title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 22: KMU v. The Director General (NEDA): Validity of the Executive ID System
primary_topics: Chapter 22 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of KMU v. The Director General (NEDA), upholding Executive Order 420, which directed government agencies and government-owned and -controlled corporations already issuing IDs to adopt a uniform data collection and format, against claims that it usurped legislative power and infringed the right to privacy.

The majority's holding on legislative power: unifying the data and standardizing the formats of ID systems that agencies already operate is purely an administrative matter falling within the President's constitutional power of control over all executive departments, bureaus and offices, and does not establish a national ID system.

The majority's holding on privacy: the right to privacy does not bar the adoption of reasonable ID systems, since the data are limited to 14 items of which only eight appear on the card, the rest being strictly confidential and outside the people's right to information -- far less sensitive than the prescription records upheld in Whalen v. Roe.

The Dissent of Justice Ynares-Santiago, joined by Justice Azcuna, that EO 420 usurped legislative functions, infringed the citizenry's right to privacy and disregarded Ople v. Torres, because a multipurpose ID's usage would be staggering and all-encompassing and the order lacked any safeguards, procedures, access limits or sanctions.
sub_topics: President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo issued EO 420 on April 13, 2005, directing all government agencies and GOCCs to adopt uniform data collection and format for their existing identification systems.
The two issues framed were whether EO 420 was a usurpation of legislative power by the President and whether it infringed on the citizen's right to privacy.
Before EO 420 the GSIS, SSS, Philhealth, the Mayor's Office, the LTO and the PRC already recorded data and issued ID cards, but the data were disparate and the IDs dissimilar.

The order enumerated its purposes -- reducing costs, achieving efficiency and reliability, ensuring compatibility, and providing convenience -- and limited the data to 14 specified items, from name and address through fingerprints and prominent distinguishing features to the Tax Identification Number.

The Court found unification purely administrative, pointing to Section 17 of Article VII, under which the President has control of all executive departments, bureaus and offices and must ensure that the laws be faithfully executed.

The power of control does not extend to the judiciary or to the independent constitutional commissions, so EO 420 reaches neither the courts nor the Comelec's voter's ID -- proof that it is not a national ID system, which would require legislation.

Three aspects of a government ID card system would require legislation: a special appropriation where none exists, compulsory coverage of all branches and all citizens, and the collection of personal data beyond what is routinely required.

On privacy the Court observed that the GSIS, SSS, LTO, Philhealth and others had issued IDs for years without complaints of privacy violation or abuse, and that petitioners had not even claimed the pre-existing systems violated their privacy.

Only eight of the 14 data appear on the card; the rest are strictly confidential under Section 6(d) of the order and, being personal matters rather than matters of public concern, are outside the right to information under Section 7 of Article III and cannot be released to the public or the press.

Whalen v. Roe was read as persuasive for upholding EO 420, the 14 routine identification data being far less sensitive and far less personal than the medical records of patients taking prescription drugs.

Ople v. Torres was distinguished: there the assailed issuance was broadly drawn and devoid of safeguards and was annulled solely because the subject matter required legislation, whereas EO 420 grants agencies no power they do not already possess.
Justice Ynares-Santiago dissented, arguing that Section 1 of Article VII merely vests executive power in the President and permits no delegation of legislative power.

She rejected the characterization of EO 420 as an internal management issuance, since a multipurpose ID could be used in any and all conceivable governmental and even private transactions, its scope of usage being staggering and all-encompassing.

She read AO 308 and EO 420 as similar in effect and intent despite their different wording, quoting Ople v. Torres that no citizen will refuse the card because no one can avoid dealing with government.

She traced the right to privacy as the inalienable right to be let alone, rooted in the common-law maxim of a man's house as his castle, constitutionalized in Griswold v. Connecticut and first recognized in Philippine law in Morfe v. Mutuc, noting that Philippine jurisprudence on privacy is at its infancy.

She enumerated the seven safeguards that made the New York statute in Whalen constitutional -- legislative deliberation on commission recommendation, narrow drafting, procedures for gathering, storage and retrieval, enumeration of who may access the data, and penalties for public disclosure -- and found EO 420 lacking all of them.

She warned that as computer technology and advanced information systems accelerate the erosion of personal privacy, profiles assembled from many sources may be inaccurate, outdated or misused, so the parameters for electronic files should be set by a legislative act and not by a mere executive order.

stances.claim: Achieving a unified ID system among agencies that already collect data and issue cards is purely an administrative matter within the President's power of control over all executive departments, bureaus and offices, and grants those agencies no power they do not already possess under existing laws.
stances.rhetorical_move: recharacterization of the measure as housekeeping, anchored in Section 17 of Article VII and in the pre-existing practice of the GSIS, SSS, LTO, Philhealth and others

stances.claim: EO 420 does not establish a national ID system, because the President's control does not reach the judiciary or the independent constitutional commissions; legislation would be needed for a compulsory system, for a special appropriation, or for data beyond those routinely required.
stances.rhetorical_move: boundary-drawing that names in advance the three circumstances in which legislation would in fact be indispensable

stances.claim: The right to privacy does not bar reasonable government ID systems: only eight of the 14 data appear on the card, the rest are strictly confidential and outside the right to information, and the whole set is far less sensitive and far more benign than the prescription records upheld in Whalen v. Roe.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative minimization against an American precedent, reinforced by the absence of any complaint against the pre-existing agency ID systems

stances.claim: Justice Ynares-Santiago, joined by Justice Azcuna, maintained that EO 420 usurped legislative functions, infringed the right to privacy and disregarded Ople v. Torres, because the reach of a multipurpose ID is practically inescapable and the order supplies no safeguards, procedures, access limits or sanctions such as those that saved the statute in Whalen.
stances.rhetorical_move: reported dissent arguing from effect rather than wording, and from a checklist of the safeguards the order lacks

notable_anecdotes: The chapter lists the 14 data items one by one -- down to height, weight, two index fingers and two thumbmarks, and moles or other prominent distinguishing features -- to show how bounded the system was meant to be.

The Court observed that for years the GSIS, SSS, LTO and Philhealth had been issuing ID cards with no complaint from citizens that they violated privacy, and that petitioners themselves had never claimed the pre-existing systems did so.

Whalen v. Roe is recounted at length: New York required physicians to report the names and addresses of patients receiving controlled prescription drugs into a centralized computer file, and the U.S. Supreme Court upheld it because of seven enumerated safeguards.

The Dissent quoted Ople v. Torres for the observation that no citizen will refuse to get the card because no one can avoid dealing with government, so that without it a citizen will have difficulty exercising his rights and enjoying his privileges.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 22 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests KMU v. The Director General (NEDA), the challenge to Executive Order 420, which President Arroyo issued on April 13, 2005 directing all government agencies and government-owned and -controlled corporations to adopt a uniform data collection and format for their existing identification systems. Two issues were framed: whether the order usurped legislative power and whether it infringed the citizen's right to privacy. The Court held that because the GSIS, SSS, Philhealth, the Mayor's Office, the LTO and the PRC already recorded data and issued cards, unifying those systems was purely an administrative matter within the President's power of control under Section 17 of Article VII, which also obliges her to ensure that the laws be faithfully executed. Since that control does not extend to the judiciary or to the independent constitutional commissions such as the Comelec, EO 420 does not establish a national ID system; legislation would be needed for a special appropriation, for compulsory coverage of all branches and citizens, or for data beyond those routinely required. On privacy, the Court noted that agencies had issued IDs for years without complaint, that the data were limited to 14 items of which only eight appear on the card, and that the remainder were strictly confidential under Section 6(d) and therefore outside the right to information on matters of public concern. Measured against Whalen v. Roe, in which the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the centralized reporting of patients receiving controlled prescription drugs, the 14 routine items were far less sensitive and far more benign, while Ople v. Torres was distinguished as having annulled a broadly drawn issuance devoid of safeguards solely because its subject matter required legislation. Justice Ynares-Santiago, joined by Justice Azcuna, dissented: a multipurpose ID's scope of usage would be staggering and all-encompassing, no citizen could avoid it, Philippine privacy jurisprudence was at its infancy, and EO 420 supplied none of the safeguards, procedures, access limits or sanctions that had saved the statute in Whalen, so the parameters for such electronic files should be set by legislation rather than by a mere executive order.
